stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIPS FROM RECORD AS RETAIL SALES POST BIGGEST DROP SINCE 2025
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.17% to 7,786 Friday, pulling back from Thursday's record close above 7,800, after July retail sales dropped 0.6% month-over-month -- the sharpest decline since May 2025 and well below the roughly +0.1% consensus. A preliminary University of Michigan reading showed consumer sentiment cooling further in August as households cited both the spending pullback and lingering inflation worries. The index still closed out a third straight weekly gain.
stories.explain: A 0.6% monthly drop in retail sales is a hard growth signal because it's actual spending, not a survey, and motor vehicles (-1.8%) and nonstore/online retail (-2.2%) led the decline while necessities like food services (+0.5%) held up -- a pattern more consistent with consumers pulling back on discretionary and big-ticket purchases than a broad-based recession. That composition matters for the Fed: a narrow, discretionary-led slowdown is easier to look through than a collapse in essentials, which is part of why today's equity reaction was a 0.17% dip rather than a disorderly selloff even after the biggest miss in over a year.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD CLIMBS TO 4.70% AS U.S. SAYS IRAN PORT BLOCKADE COULD RUN 'INDEFINITELY'
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 5 basis points to 4.696% Friday after the U.S. said its naval blockade of Iranian ports could continue indefinitely, even as traders simultaneously digested the weak retail sales print. Oil held its geopolitical premium on the news, with WTI near $82 and Brent near $87-88.
stories.explain: Normally a growth-negative surprise like today's retail sales miss pulls nominal yields down, since it raises the odds of Fed easing and drives flight-to-quality buying. Today it didn't, because the blockade news works through the other half of the yield equation: it raises breakeven inflation expectations by threatening sustained upward pressure on oil, which nominal yields have to price in even as real growth expectations soften. When a supply-side shock and a demand-side shock hit the same day, they pull the same yield in opposite directions -- and today the inflation-risk leg won, which is exactly the kind of stagflationary tension the Fed has to navigate into its September 16 meeting.

stories.headline: BROADCOM SINKS 6% ON $370B AI DEBT-FINANCING QUESTION, DRAGS NASDAQ 100 LOWER
stories.body: Broadcom shares fell roughly 6% Friday after BofA Securities estimated the company's AI chip-financing vehicle could balloon to $370 billion in senior debt by 2029, including about $150 billion of new issuance in 2027 alone. The Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.13% to 30,046 as the selloff rippled through semiconductors, even as AMD gained roughly 4% on a bullish Baird price target.
stories.explain: The $370 billion figure isn't debt sitting on Broadcom's own balance sheet -- it's projected debt in an off-balance-sheet financing vehicle that funds AI chip leases, with Broadcom backstopping some of the customer lease obligations. Markets still punish the stock because a backstop is a contingent liability: if lessees can't pay, Broadcom absorbs the shortfall, so the real economic leverage is larger than the reported balance sheet shows. This is the same structural question hanging over the broader AI capex boom -- how much of the spending is funded by vendor financing and special-purpose vehicles rather than customer cash flow -- and today's move shows investors starting to price that risk into individual names rather than treating AI capex as a uniformly positive catalyst.

stories.headline: GOLD HOLDS NEAR $4,432, UP 1.2% AS WEAKER DOLLAR AND FED-HOLD BETS BUOY BULLION
stories.body: Gold gained about 1.2% to roughly $4,432 an ounce Friday as the dollar index slipped 0.25% to 99.64 and traders raised bets that the Fed will leave rates unchanged at its September meeting rather than hike, building on Thursday's benign core CPI and today's soft retail sales.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its relative attractiveness moves inversely with real (inflation-adjusted) Treasury yields and with the dollar, since a weaker dollar makes dollar-priced bullion cheaper for foreign buyers. Today both levers moved in gold's favor: falling hike odds cap how far real yields can rise even as nominal yields ticked up on the blockade story, and DXY's slide to 99.64 added a currency tailwind. That combination -- softer growth data lowering the odds of further tightening while a geopolitical premium keeps a safe-haven bid alive -- is the same setup that's driven roughly a month of gold strength.

stories.headline: OIL FIRMS NEAR $82 WTI AS INDEFINITE IRAN PORT BLOCKADE OFFSETS WEAK DEMAND OUTLOOK
stories.body: WTI crude rose about 1.3% to near $82 a barrel and Brent held near $87-88 Friday, as the U.S. Navy's blockade of Iranian ports -- now described as open-ended -- kept a geopolitical floor under prices even after the IEA and OPEC's recent downward revisions to 2026 demand growth.
stories.explain: Oil is being pulled by two forces that don't net out cleanly: a bearish demand signal from IEA/OPEC forecast cuts that traders can act on immediately by selling futures, and a supply-side risk premium tied to the Strait of Hormuz corridor, which carries roughly a fifth of global seaborne crude. An 'indefinite' blockade removes the option of pricing the risk as temporary, so the premium gets embedded further out the futures curve rather than fading -- which is why WTI is up on the day even though the demand backdrop hasn't improved at all.

stories.headline: TRANSFER PORTAL AFTERSHOCKS CONTINUE AS FIFTH-YEAR RULING RESHAPES ROSTERS INTO FALL
stories.body: North Carolina guard Seth Trimble is transferring to Louisville, the latest ripple from the federal fifth-year eligibility ruling that triggered a special Aug. 3-10 transfer window. Arizona, Tennessee and Gonzaga are among the programs still rounding out veteran-heavy rosters, and preseason Top 25 projections continue shifting as programs finalize their 15-man rosters heading toward fall practice.

stories.headline: STOUDEMIRE, DOC RIVERS, D'ANTONI HEADLINE 2026 HALL OF FAME CLASS ENSHRINED TONIGHT
stories.body: The Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame formally enshrines its 2026 class Saturday at 7 PM ET in Springfield, Mass. Six-time All-Star Amar'e Stoudemire is the class's lone NBA player, joined by Bucks coach Doc Rivers, offensive innovator Mike D'Antoni (1,199 career wins, two-time Coach of the Year), Candace Parker and Gonzaga's Mark Few among nine total inductees.

stories.headline: PRESEASON WEEK 1 WRAPS WITH SEVEN-GAME SATURDAY SLATE; WATSON, SANDERS BOTH PLAY FOR BROWNS
stories.body: Saturday's seven-game slate closes out Preseason Week 1, headlined by Cleveland's QB battle between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders against Chicago and the Cowboys-Seahawks primetime finale at Lumen Field (8 PM ET, NFL Network). New Orleans took a hit Friday when DT Bryan Bresee and G Dillon Radunz both landed on injured reserve with season-ending knee injuries against Jacksonville.

stories.headline: ALABAMA STILL WITHOUT A STARTING QB AS DEBOER'S CAMP TIMELINE SLIPS
stories.body: More than a week into fall camp, Kalen DeBoer has yet to name a starter between redshirt junior Austin Mack and redshirt freshman Keelon Russell, despite hoping for a decision roughly a week and a half in -- a deadline that's now come and gone. Ohio State opens camp as the national title betting favorite with QB Julian Sayin and WR Jeremiah Smith back under new OC Arthur Smith.

sports.detail: Fall camp continues under third-year coach Jedd Fisch; Saturday's practice runs 5:45 PM, part of a stretch focused on installs and evaluating new faces. Mock Game and picture day is Aug. 22; season opens vs. Washington State -- Sunday, Sept. 6, 1 PM PT on NBC, Husky Stadium.

UW's 15-man roster for 2026-27 is complete after landing Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno, a 6-foot-7 Bosnian guard. Danny Sprinkle enters Year 3 leaning on returner Wesley Yates III (12.9 ppg) and five portal additions after last year's 16-17, non-tournament finish.

Seattle opens the preseason at home vs. Dallas tonight, 6 PM MT / 8 PM ET at Lumen Field (NFL Network) -- the defending Super Bowl champions' first game action of the year. CB Terrion Arnold is finalizing a deal with the club, and rookie RB Jadarian Price has drawn praise in camp.

Detroit's 2026-27 schedule opens at home vs. Boston on Oct. 20 in the league's opening-night tripleheader (3 PM ET, NBC). Isaiah Stewart is now in Memphis, opening a bigger frontcourt role for Paul Reed, while All-NBA Third Team center Jalen Duren remains unsigned in restricted free agency.

Seattle dropped the series opener at Houston 10-7 in 10 innings Friday after Christian Walker's go-ahead three-run homer. The two teams play again tonight, 5:10 PM MT at Daikin Park, with Emerson Hancock on the mound against Hayden Wesneski.

watchlist: FOMC meeting Sept. 16 -- rate-hold odds rising after soft retail sales and July's benign core CPI (2.5% YoY)
Seahawks preseason opener vs. Cowboys -- tonight, 6 PM MT, Lumen Field, NFL Network
Mariners at Astros -- tonight, 5:10 PM MT, Houston
Washington State expected to name starting QB by Aug. 24
August PPI report -- Thursday, Sept. 10, 8:30 AM ET

deepDive.title: Why 'Indefinite' Reshapes the Oil Futures Curve, Not Just the Spot Price
content: WTI is holding near $82 for a second straight session while equity and bond markets sit closed for the weekend, but the U.S. Navy's blockade of Iranian ports remains officially open-ended -- and that word choice matters more than it sounds. A trader pricing a disruption expected to resolve within weeks behaves very differently than one pricing a disruption with no defined endpoint. The difference doesn't show up in today's headline spot price, which barely moved from Friday's close. It shows up in the shape of the futures curve stretching months and years into 2027 and 2028.

Oil futures curves normally slope based on storage costs and expected supply-demand balance, and a temporary shock produces steep backwardation -- near-term contracts priced well above deferred ones -- because traders expect the disruption's premium to fade as it resolves. An indefinite shock flattens that decay pattern. Instead of pricing a spike-and-fade, the market starts embedding sustained risk further out the curve, since 2027 and 2028 contracts can no longer assume mean reversion to a pre-crisis baseline. That's a structurally different bet than a short squeeze, and it changes who is exposed: airlines, shippers and refiners hedging multi-year forward costs, not just spot buyers.

The historical parallel is the 1973 Arab oil embargo, when prices near-quadrupled from roughly $3 to $12 a barrel in a matter of months and fed directly into double-digit U.S. inflation by 1974. Energy carries a direct CPI weight of only around 6-7%, but its indirect pass-through -- transportation costs, plastics, fertilizer, and ultimately food -- is what turns an oil shock into a broad inflation problem rather than a contained one. The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine offers a more recent, smaller-scale version: Brent jumped from roughly $95 to near $130 within weeks, and the energy component of U.S. CPI rose over 40% year-over-year that spring, dragging headline inflation well above core.

That pass-through lag is exactly why Friday's tape looked contradictory -- yields up, gold up, equities only modestly lower -- and why it matters heading into the next CPI print and the Fed's September 16 decision. Weak retail sales argue for easing; an indefinite blockade argues energy costs still have room to work through the pipeline into headline inflation over the coming months. Watch the CPI energy subcomponent specifically, not just the headline number: if it starts climbing the way it did in 2022, the Fed's 'hold' bias gets a lot harder to defend.
